title: Scalp acoustoelectric recording of human cortex through a 6 mm ultrasound focus at diagnostic intensity needs about 100,000 trials or more unless neural coupling is ten times that of saline
abstract: Scalp electrodes cannot record human cortical activity through a 6 mm ultrasound focus in a practical time at the diagnostic ultrasound intensity limit, unless neural tissue couples pressure and current about ten times more strongly than saline. This matters because several groups develop acoustoelectric recording as a non-invasive method with millimetre and millisecond resolution, but no one had calculated the full signal budget for real neural sources. In acoustoelectric recording, focused ultrasound changes the electrical resistivity of tissue at the focus (constant K, about 4e-10 per pascal in saline), so that local currents appear at the ultrasound frequency. We used a new cell-level theory, cable models of 31 reconstructed human pyramidal neurons, a 3D finite-volume check, a four-shell head model at 0.5 MHz, and published values for safety limits, tissue properties and cortical current strength. At ultrasound frequencies the lead field (the sensitivity pattern of the electrodes) goes through dendritic membranes. Thus, for activity wider than the focus, the modulated current inside neurons cancels the modulated return current outside them: the ionic signal falls to less than 0.2 percent of the conventional prediction. What remains is a term from the pressure dependence of membrane capacitance, and its size has not been measured. For a strong response (0.5 nA m per mm2), a 0.5 MHz focus with a 5.6 mm pressure width, 720 mW/cm2 continuous ultrasound, a coupling coefficient equal to K and the best scalp electrode, the signal is 0.22 nV and the noise is 2.95 nV per root hertz. Detection needs 440,000 trials at 10 ms resolution (100,000 with an ideal electrode array), or 2.4 hours per focal spot for a steady response. One thousand trials are sufficient only at 16 mm resolution (12 mm with an ideal array), or with a coefficient 10 to 21 times K. A published in vivo mouse recording implies a coefficient of roughly 5 to 20 times K. If this applies to human tissue, 1,000 trials are sufficient at 5 to 7 mm. Electrodes within 3 to 5 mm of the focus need 60 to 4,300 trials with K. The main limitations are the unmeasured coefficient, a spherical head model, and mouse values read from figures.
